extracted.intended_audience: pipeline operators, pipeline industry stakeholders, and regulatory compliance staff (PHMSA-regulated gas and hazardous liquid pipeline operators)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory criteria for defining, detecting, identifying, notifying, and mitigating pipeline ruptures (including RMV installation and alternative technologies) for gas and hazardous liquid pipelines under PHMSA's final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leak detection and right-of-way inspection requirements for hazardous liquid pipelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators of hazardous liquid pipelines have been required since 2002 to evaluate and install leak detection systems in HCAs; October 2019 regulations require that all hazardous liquid pipelines, even those outside of HCAs, have an effective system for detecting leaks; hazardous liquid pipeline operators are required to inspect the surface conditions of their rights-of-way every 3 weeks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA emphasizes robust leak detection on PHMSA-jurisdictional pipelines and mandates periodic surface inspections (every 3 weeks) of rights-of-way to identify leaks or anomalies. This is a standing regulatory obligation separate from RMV requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patrol and leak survey intervals for gas distribution and transmission pipelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Gas distribution pipeline operators are required by §§ 192.722 and 192.723 to conduct periodic patrols and leak surveys; gas transmission pipeline operators are required by § 192.705 to conduct periodic patrols and by § 192.706 to conduct leak surveys twice per year in Class 3 locations and quarterly for Class 4 locations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These existing regulatory intervals establish baseline monitoring expectations and inform how rupture detection/identification obligations integrate with routine patrols and leak surveys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of RMV/alternative technology requirement to newly constructed or entirely replaced pipelines (>= 6 inches)
rubrics_metrics.description: PHMSA proposed (and in final rule) to require that all valves on newly constructed or entirely replaced onshore gas transmission and hazardous liquid pipelines with diameters greater than or equal to 6 inches be RMVs or an alternative equivalent technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operators may propose alternative equivalent technologies but must demonstrate equivalence; manual valves as alternatives require demonstration that RMV installation is not economically, technically, or operationally feasible. Valves must meet the rupture-mitigation standards in the cited regulatory sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operator notification to PHMSA when using alternative equivalent technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators seeking to use an alternative equivalent technology in lieu of an RMV must submit a notification to PHMSA demonstrating that their preferred technology would provide an equivalent level of safety to an RMV.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the alternative is a manual valve, the operator must also demonstrate that installation of an RMV is not economically, technically, or operationally feasible. The alternative must meet the new rupture-mitigation standards proposed in the applicable sections (§ 192.634 / § 195.418).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation of valve-installation requirements to Type A gas gathering pipelines (exemption for Type B/C)
rubrics_metrics.description: PHMSA narrowed application of the RMV and alternative equivalent technology installation requirements to Type A gas gathering pipelines only; Type B and Type C gas gathering pipelines are explicitly exempted from those requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justification is based on differing risk profiles: Type A operate at higher pressures and in higher population densities (Class 2–4), presenting greater public safety risk. PHMSA may consider future rulemaking for other gathering types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception for new or entirely replaced Type A gas gathering pipelines in Class 2 with PIR ≤ 150 ft
rubrics_metrics.description: PHMSA provides an exception from the valve installation requirements if an operator can demonstrate that a rupture on a new or entirely replaced Type A gas gathering pipeline in Class 2 locations would yield a PIR (Potential Impact Radius) of 150 feet or less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operators can use PIR analysis to justify an exception; the rule narrows requirements recognizing variable consequences tied to PIR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulated rural hazardous liquid gathering lines and water-crossing valve requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators of regulated rural hazardous liquid gathering lines must comply with part 195 provisions; PHMSA is requiring that operators of regulated rural gathering lines that cross bodies of water greater than 100 feet wide (high-water-mark to high-water-mark) install RMVs or alternative equivalent technologies in accordance with § 195.260(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA historically required extra valves near such water crossings; the final rule applies the RMV requirements to these specific crossings to address environmental risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: RMV requirement for newly constructed and entirely replaced low-stress, rural hazardous liquid pipelines (>= 6 inches)
rubrics_metrics.description: All newly constructed and entirely replaced low-stress, rural hazardous liquid pipelines with diameter of six inches or greater, including low-stress hazardous liquid pipelines in rural areas, must install RMVs pursuant to this rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA acknowledged lower rupture likelihood below 20% SMYS but concluded leaks can still cause significant environmental damage; the LPAC recommendation for exception was not adopted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of gas distribution pipelines from RMV requirements (limited provisions apply)
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirements pertaining to RMVs or alternative equivalent technologies do not apply to gas distribution pipelines; the only requirements in this rule intended to apply to gas distribution pipelines are § 192.615 for contacting 9-1-1 call centers and § 192.617 pertaining to post-incident analysis and implementation of lessons learned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA may study and evaluate appropriate measures for distribution pipelines in future rulemaking; extending RMV-like requirements to distribution would require additional notice and comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: 'notification of potential rupture' (replacement for proposed 'rupture')
rubrics_metrics.description: PHMSA changed the proposed definition of 'rupture' to 'notification of potential rupture' describing events involving indicia of an uncontrolled release, including: (1) a release observed/reported to the operator that may represent an unintentional/uncontrolled release; (2) an unanticipated or unplanned pressure loss of 10 percent or greater within 15 minutes (unless operator documents need for a higher threshold); or (3) an unexplained flow rate/pressure/instrumentation/equipment change that may be representative of such an event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA moved detailed criteria into operative sections (§§ 192.635 and 195.417). The change recognizes that operator actions should often be initiated on notification of indicia rather than waiting for confirmed 'rupture.' Industry commenters requested flexibility; PHMSA retained the 10%-within-15-minutes criterion but allowed operators to document alternative thresholds when justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operator ability to document alternative pressure/flow thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Because operators may have conditions causing pressure/flow fluctuations in excess of the 10%/15-minute threshold, PHMSA permits operators to document in their written procedures the need for alternative pressure-loss-rate (or flow-change) thresholds due to unique pipeline flow dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA does not require operators to submit these written procedures to PHMSA in advance for approval. The qualifying language that any such pressure loss must be 'unanticipated or unexplained' also helps avoid routine events triggering notifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rupture identification methodology and written procedures requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: PHMSA requires each operator to have written procedures specifying its methodology for identifying a rupture on receipt of a 'notification of potential rupture'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA declined the NPRM's 10-minute global identification deadline but expects operators to document how they will identify ruptures 'as soon as practicable.' Procedures should include common-sense elements and may waive on-scene investigation when: multiple/recurring instrument indications; pressure drops significantly in excess of minimum thresholds; or reports of rupture indicia from credible on-scene sources (e.g., police, fire, on/off-duty operator personnel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing for RMV operation following rupture identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators installing RMVs must close RMVs 'as soon as practicable,' but not to exceed 30 minutes from rupture identification, to isolate a ruptured pipeline segment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NPRM proposed a 40-minute limit; Committees recommended 30 minutes; PHMSA codified demanding timelines—operation 'as soon as practicable,' with a 30-minute upper bound—to reduce delays in mitigation while allowing operational flexibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rupture identification vs notification distinction and when response actions may be keyed
rubrics_metrics.description: PHMSA recharacterized the NPRM's 'rupture' definition to 'notification of potential rupture' and distinguishes between initiating response actions on notification versus on confirmed rupture identification; PHMSA considered but did not adopt initiating RMV operations on mere notification of potential rupture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA remains concerned about delayed identification in past incidents; however, to avoid over-triggering valve closures and to allow documentation-based flexibility, PHMSA requires procedures for identification and keying RMV operation timelines to operator identification rather than to initial notification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of detailed criteria in operative sections (enforceability and clarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: PHMSA found including detailed criteria in definition sections unwieldy and instead located the criteria for 'notification of potential rupture' in operative regulatory sections (§§ 192.635 and 195.417) to improve clarity and enforceability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This organizational choice mirrors prior approaches (e.g., definition of 'unusually sensitive area') and makes requirements and criteria actionable in the regulatory text rather than tucked inside definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicia of rupture to be considered (explosions, fires, instrumentation, credible reports)
rubrics_metrics.description: PHMSA clarified definitional criteria to identify indicia of rupture, explicitly identifying indicia including explosions and fires in the immediate vicinity of a pipeline, multiple/recurring instrument indications (pressure readings, alarms), significant pressure drops, and reports from credible on-scene sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These indicia can justify prompt response actions and may allow waiver of on-scene investigation when documented in written procedures. PHMSA expects operators to weigh multiple indicia collectively to determine whether a rupture is in progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with incident/accident reporting definitions (not codified)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters requested alignment between the regulatory definition of rupture and the definition used in PHMSA's incident/accident reporting instructions (which state rupture occurs when pipeline 'burst, split, or broken and the operation of the pipeline facility is immediately impaired'). PHMSA acknowledged the value but declined to codify a regulatory 'rupture' definition in this final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA may consider ensuring consistency in future rulemakings; for now, the rule uses 'notification of potential rupture' and places criteria in operative sections, with the intent to avoid inconsistency in tracking rule effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of operator-specific rupture notification criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters recommended allowing operators to establish specific rupture-notification criteria for individual pipelines based on unique operating environments rather than one-size-fits-all numerical thresholds; PHMSA permits operators to document alternative thresholds in procedures and expects tailored methodologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA retained a default numerical criterion (10% over 15 minutes) as appropriate in many investigated ruptures, but explicitly allows documented, justified deviations to reflect operational realities and avoid false alarms or unnecessary closures.
